items.desc: On May 12, 2023, the authorities ordered the evacuation of the village of Brienz/Brinzauls in the canton of Grisons, as a rapid slide of the slope above the village appeared imminent. However, it took its time. It was not until the night of June 15–16 that around 1.2 million cubic meters (1.6 million cubic yards) of rock and debris slid toward the village, narrowly missing it.

items.title: 11,000-year-old clay fragments reveal early experiments in pottery-making
items.desc: Long before pottery became commonplace in Southwest Asia, people living beside the Upper Tigris were experimenting with ways to turn clay into containers.

items.title: Crushes and other injuries: What science tells us about grieving a heartbreak
items.desc: Something funny happened at work, and there is one person you really want to tell. You stare at their name in your contact list. You know that if you call, no one will answer. They're gone.

items.title: Beyond food: Bran-based gels show potential for targeted drug delivery
items.desc: When it comes to colon health, the benefits of wheat and rye bran in whole-grain foods are well known. Now researchers in Sweden have shown how these fibers may have a therapeutic use, too. A new study published in the journal Biomacromolecules demonstrates the potential to use bran fiber for direct delivery of drugs to treat colon diseases like ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease or colorectal cancer.

items.title: Glass does surprising things when stretched 1 atom wide. The discovery could help shrink electronics
items.desc: Smartwatches worn on millions of wrists today pack vastly more processing power than the computers that helped Apollo astronauts land on the moon. But the scientific drive to go tiny has come at a cost: It means heat, electricity and energy now have much less room to flow through devices.

items.title: Bennu asteroid analysis suggests unexpected origins for organics in space
items.desc: Samples from the Bennu asteroid, which is currently more than 200 million miles (322 million kilometers) from Earth, and the Murchison meteorite, which fell to Earth in 1969, both contain molecules that build proteins necessary for life. New research has found that the molecules may have formed through the same process but originated far from one another in the solar system.

items.title: New strategy boosts iron-based single-atom catalysts for Fenton-like reactions
items.desc: Researchers at the Xinjiang Technical Institute of Physics and Chemistry (XTIPC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) have developed a core-shell confined iron-based single-atom catalyst that combines high Fenton-like catalytic activity with structural stability, enabling nearly complete removal of 2,4-dichlorophenol (2,4-DCP) within 20 minutes under mildly acidic conditions.

items.title: The faces of iridium: One metal, many reactions
items.desc: The same metal can have many faces, and each tells a different chemical story. At the atomic scale, those different faces can push the same reaction along very different paths.

items.title: III-nitride device integrates sensing and memory for in-sensor computing
items.desc: A new study published in Nature Materials reports that researchers have developed an aluminum gallium nitride device that combines light detection, memory and basic processing by controlling charge at polarization interfaces. The device can detect light at the nanowatt-per-square-centimeter level and operate stably at temperatures up to 300°C.

items.title: A standard shortcut, used since the 1970s, hides a magneto-optic effect in ordinary glass fiber
items.desc: For more than 50 years, engineers have described light in optical fiber using a convenient shortcut, one that works so well it is rarely questioned. Engineers at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg, South Africa, have now shown that this shortcut hides a small but real effect. A magnet placed beside a multimode fiber, rather than along it, can change the light traveling inside.

items.title: New algorithm improves phase readout for space-based gravitational wave detection
items.desc: In a study published in Optics Communications, a research group led by Yu Tao from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics (CIOMP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences proposed a new analytical phase readout algorithm for deep frequency modulation interferometry (DFMI).

items.title: Wonder and ore: A spectacular new view from space maps Australia's mineral wealth
items.desc: A new tool that uses detailed satellite images to help unlock Australia's mineral wealth has been unveiled.

items.title: Research snapshot: The use of icons in aphasia-friendly texts
items.desc: Pictorial reading supports, such as icons, can help people with aphasia better comprehend the material and enjoy the reading process. But exactly what type of icon is most helpful?

items.title: RipEye flags possible rip currents in beach photos within seconds
items.desc: Rip currents remain one of Australia's deadliest beach hazards, contributing to 47% of the 66 beach drowning deaths recorded in the 2025 National Drowning Report.

items.title: Roman-era 'frog feast' near Cambridge was the work of owls, bone analysis suggests
items.desc: Around 1,800 years ago, over 9,000 bones, mainly from frogs, ended up in an Iron Age/Roman gully near Cambridge. When archaeologists first dug them up, speculation soon followed. Were these the remains of a Roman frog feast or perhaps the skeletal aftermath of a ritual?

items.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
items.desc: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.

items.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
items.desc: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

items.title: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.

items.title: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low
items.desc: Even when bad cholesterol is brought down to healthy levels, some people remain at risk of heart attacks, and scientists may have discovered why. Researchers identified two types of fat-carrying particles that appear to promote inflammation and damage blood vessels through mechanisms beyond cholesterol buildup.

items.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

items.title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
items.desc: A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater. Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.

items.title: NASA’s CHAPEA Mars crew finally emerges after more than a year in isolation
items.desc: After more than a year of simulated life on Mars, four NASA volunteers have finally emerged from isolation, bringing a remarkable space exploration experiment to an end. Their experiences growing food, conserving resources, and overcoming Mars-like challenges could help NASA prepare for humanity's future on the Moon and Mars.

items.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
items.desc: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

items.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
items.desc: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.

items.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.

items.title: NASA reveals bold new plan to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028
items.desc: NASA has revealed an accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing competing lunar landers and a crucial orbital test scheduled for 2027. Faster rocket preparations, new lightweight spacesuits, and redesigned missions could help pave the way for a permanent lunar presence and future human exploration of Mars.

items.title: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay
items.desc: CERN scientists have finally found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it happens only once in roughly 10 billion decays, ending a search spanning more than 40 years. The breakthrough could help physicists uncover hidden particles and forces that lie beyond the reach of today's most powerful accelerators.

items.title: A radical theory says the universe is twice as old as we thought
items.desc: A provocative new cosmological model suggests the Universe could be 26.7 billion years old and might not need dark matter or dark energy to explain its behavior. University of Ottawa researchers tested the theory against several major astronomical observations, finding that it could explain galaxy rotation, cosmic expansion, and the formation of early elements.

items.title: Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images
items.desc: A breakthrough in telescope imaging could reveal countless alien worlds that have been hiding in plain sight. Scientists developed a new technique that uses a digital twin of the James Webb Space Telescope to remove the overwhelming glare of stars, making faint exoplanets two to 15 times easier to detect than with conventional methods. The technology has already uncovered a previously hidden planet in existing telescope data and could reveal many more.

items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
items.desc: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

items.title: It’s the Corruption, Stupid
items.desc: Fed up with Donald Trump and his family's blatant profiteering, Americans dealt Republicans a resounding defeat in this month’s midterm elections. Democrats won by linking corruption to the cost-of-living crisis, but the party’s establishment remains compromised and must clean house before 2028.

items.title: AI Investors Have Overlooked Obvious Risks
items.desc: Prior to the US midterm elections on November 3, financial markets had been treating generative AI as some kind of unstoppable force that could not be hampered by higher interest rates or political and social resistance. But now reality may be setting in.

items.title: The Mismeasure of Privacy
items.desc: Over the past few decades, we have adopted a new framework for thinking about privacy that centers our experience in the digital realm, conflates privacy with secrecy, and fails to account for the insecurity surveillance generates. As a result, even privacy advocates often undermine their own cause.

items.title: The Right Lessons From Brazil and the US
items.desc: One lesson progressives in both countries cannot afford to ignore is that recent election results do not amount to a mandate. Neither the Democrats in the US nor President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s Workers' Party in Brazil are offering a vision voters can get excited about.

items.title: A Russian Bribe the Size of Europe
items.desc: US President Donald Trump is willing to sacrifice Ukraine in exchange for lucrative oil and gas deals with Russia, but this bargain is bound to backfire spectacularly. Vladimir Putin has a long record of betraying his business partners, and once he gets what he wants from Trump, Europe will be his next target.

items.title: Will Anthropic’s IPO Lead to Better AI Regulation?
items.desc: When frontier AI labs go public, ordinary people’s investments and pensions become tied to their valuations and stock prices. While excessive regulation could undermine a firm’s growth, catastrophic accidents caused by inadequate safety measures could do the same—and wipe out shareholder value.

items.title: A Minimum Basic Income Is Not Enough
items.desc: The rise of AI is concentrating wealth and political power in fewer and fewer hands, making extreme inequality a threat to democracy itself. A universal basic share that gives ordinary people a portion of global profits could help narrow the growing gap between billionaires and everyone else.

items.title: Scott Bessent’s Risky Short-Termism
items.desc: The US Treasury secretary's commitment to accelerate buybacks of longer-term debt and issue more short-term debt in their place promises significant budgetary savings. But if borrowing costs rise, what happens in the T-bill market won’t stay in the T-bill market.

items.title: Why Trump Crowned the Man Who Cost Him Congress
items.desc: By appointing Stephen Miller to be his chief of staff, US President Donald Trump has revealed what he cannot give up after decisive midterm losses. The moral depravity of one of the most widely reviled members of his administration is the citadel he will defend until the end.

items.title: Why Politicians Love Stimulus Checks
items.desc: Stimulus checks sent to households promise to supercharge the economy, but much of the money simply sits in people's bank accounts. They are popular with voters but do little to address the underlying causes of economic downturns and leave future generations to foot the bill.

items.title: Who’s Winning (and Who’s Losing) the Ocean? — Marie-May Jeremie
items.desc: Ahead of COP31, PS sat down with Marie-May Jeremie, Minister of Environment, Climate, Energy and Natural Resources of the Republic of Seychelles, to discuss the logic of “blue” economic development. Watch as she describes the deeply personal stakes for small island states, and calls on the global community to support their efforts.

items.title: The Midterms Won’t Change Much for US Allies
items.desc: Even if the Democrats’ midterm victory marks the beginning of the end of the Trump administration’s “America First” approach to foreign affairs, it does not augur the return of a consistent, reliable US foreign policy. America's friends and allies around the world will have to continue to hedge their bets.

items.title: Revolts of the Young
items.desc: Young protesters have taken to the streets in France, India, Serbia, and several other countries, rising up against corrupt mainstream parties and economic inequality. But their efforts to improve liberal democracy will likely be overshadowed by the far right’s far more organized efforts to seize power.

items.title: What the ILO Can Teach a Divided World
items.desc: In a world where compromise is held in contempt, collective action is increasingly difficult. The International Labour Organization’s decades-long record of bringing workers, employers, and governments to the negotiating table has been exceptional in this regard, demonstrating the necessity and potential of multilateralism.

items.title: The Five Stages of AI Grief
items.desc: Like those diagnosed with a terminal illness, humanity is being forced through the stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance as AI’s capabilities and potential rapidly expand. But there is a crucial difference: AI and its uses are not outside our control.
